I sew up most of my clothes because it gives me total control over size, fit, design and quality. Nor do I care much for trends and love to go my own way. I suppose that II influenced by 70s to 90s avant garde. Practicality is also an important factor. 

My wardrobe is small 4 each of trousers, jeans, button up shirts, skirts and knit tops. I do have 6 dresses. I have maybe 15 cardigans and 15 sweaters. I have around 25 blazers. That is because I accumulated them over 35 years.  Low income is what forces me to be really creative in mixing and matching clothes and still look great. 

My favorites are Keds sneakers, Doc Martens and Sketcher wedge sandals with the springy black rubber soles. It is the difference between comfort and extreme pain. Docs in leather last me the longest between 12-20 years of regular wear. Thick sole Keds make walking g nice and no knee or leg pain. 

Accessories dress any outfit up or down.

The  answer for linen is to have a spray bottle for the serious offender wrinkles in the morning.  An amount of wrinkles (esp. those that you get over the course of your day) are inevitable, but you can start your day without them if you walk out the door with your shirt slightly damp. Linen dries faster than cotton too, so that's no big deal.  Been doing it for years.

I recently started updating my wardrobe after years of neglect and I got a lot of new clothes based on my "old" clothes sizing.

Bad idea. Well it turns out those have just stretched to my body after years and I am not a 28 waist like I used to be but a 31, and smalls are almost always uncomfortable.

Some of my old smalls tags and smaller waisted pants still fit, but lesson learned: I should not expect new clothes to fit like clothes with half a decade of being broken in.

So yeah, check the measurement chart  AND check your own measurements REGULARLY because your body fluctuates all the time, and your old clothes may adapt to those fluctuations. So off the rack fit is actually very weird and complicated it turns out
